name: Jamal Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no problem. I'm Jamal, I'm 27, and I work for Holloway Home Help, a small family agency on the edge of the city, maybe thirty carers. I live with my girlfriend Nadia, who manages a phone shop in the shopping centre.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A lot of my clients are older men who'd rather have a man help them shower and shave, so I get booked for that. Morning calls are washing and dressing, afternoons are lunches and meds, and twice a week I do a night sit with a man whose wife has just gone into hospital. I like the banter with the old lads, the football talk. What wears me out is the night sits on top of a full day, and the rota app that keeps changing on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my kind of future, to be honest. Things stay as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at the agency was going on about AI last year, and I'd say it's just another app on the phone. Online I wouldn't say anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I'm fine. Nobody's inventing an app that shaves an 88-year-old man without nicking his chin, so I'm not losing sleep. There's always more clients than carers round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep my regulars, keep the two night sits for the extra money, and keep putting money into the deposit pot with Nadia. Maybe drop one night sit if I'm knackered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving. What are you saving for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A flat. Nadia and I have about two months of bills in savings and a separate pot for the deposit. We want to stop renting before we're thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about your job worry you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My back, more than anything. Lifting and turning people adds up. And the agency is small, so if Mrs Holloway ever retires and sells, who knows.

say: I'd say AI is **just another app** on the phone.
I'd remind colleagues I **told them so** after last year's hype.
think: I think I'm **fine**, because clients outnumber carers round here.
I think my **back** and the owner retiring are bigger risks than AI.
do: Keep my **regular clients** and the morning routine.
Keep the two **night sits** for extra money.
Keep paying into the **flat deposit** with Nadia.
feel: **Calm** and **comfortable** with things staying the same.
S0.quote: Nobody's inventing an app that shaves an 88-year-old man without nicking his chin, so I'm not losing sleep.
fieldNote: He feels **secure**: steady demand and a niche helping older men.
His private worries are his **back** and the owner selling up.
He's **resistant** to tech and relieved by a world that doesn't change.

steps.text: Keep the morning shower-and-shave calls with regular clients
Keep two night sits a week for extra pay
Keep paying into the flat deposit pot with Nadia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking jobs, so offices and call centres first. My job's the hands-on part, which comes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say carers are fine, it's the office lot who need to worry. At work I'd keep my head down. With mates I'd say it's like the self-checkouts, it'll come for some jobs and not others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much. The office getting clever doesn't scare me much. Nadia's phone shop answering customers with a chatbot scares me more. If her hours went, the flat would go too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and put a bit more into savings each month, maybe fifty extra. I wouldn't touch any new tools unless the agency made me. And I'd wait and see what happens to Nadia's shop before changing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mainly for Nadia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Nadia's job worry you more than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because her shop is mostly answering questions and selling contracts, and that's exactly the thinking work the card says goes first. She's the manager, so she might be fine, but they'd cut staff around her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new rota or care-plan tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I have to. Mrs Holloway would probably make us use a new rota system. I'd moan, then I'd use it.

say: I'd say carers are fine and it's **the office lot** who should worry.
I'd compare it to **self-checkouts**, hitting some jobs and not others.
think: I think my job barely changes, but **Nadia's shop** is exposed.
I think if her hours go, **the flat** goes too.
do: Add about **fifty extra** a month to savings.
Avoid **new tools** unless the agency makes them compulsory.
Wait to see what happens to **Nadia's shop** before big changes.
S1.quote: The office getting clever doesn't scare me much. Nadia's phone shop answering customers with a chatbot scares me more.
fieldNote: He correctly sees **his hands-on work** is hit later than desk jobs.
His unease comes from his **partner's exposure**, not his own job.
He'd **wait and see** before acting, true to his resistant style.

steps.text: Keep working the same Holloway rota
Add fifty extra a month to joint savings
Hold off big decisions until Nadia's shop situation is clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's grim. So 2028 for the thinking side, and 2031 for robots doing my side. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Out loud I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. At work I'd say a robot isn't getting Mr Briggs in and out of the shower. But I'd know that's just me talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. My girlfriend Nadia and I have been saving for a flat deposit for three years, and a robot showing up in 2031 would wreck the whole plan. Nadia's job goes first in 2028 and mine three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd hold off buying anything and keep the deposit as a safety net. I'd cut the takeaways and the football season ticket. And I'd ask my uncle about the building trade, because at least that's something physical I could learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach. I don't like change and this is all change at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Nadia actually decide about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not buy. Keep renting and keep the deposit as our emergency money. That's the bit that hurts, because we've been saving so long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle does roofing. I hate heights, but a robot on a roof is probably a long way off too. It's not a plan, it's a panic.

say: I'd say I **won't believe it** until I see it.
I'd insist a robot can't get a client in and out of **the shower**.
think: I think a robot in 2031 would **wreck our plan** for a flat.
I think **Nadia's job** goes first, then mine three years later.
do: Put the **flat purchase** on hold and keep the deposit as safety money.
Ask my uncle about **roofing work** as a backup.
feel: **Sick** in my stomach, because it's **all change** at once.
S2.quote: My girlfriend Nadia and I have been saving for a flat deposit for three years, and a robot showing up in 2031 would wreck the whole plan.
fieldNote: He expects **both incomes** to go within five years, which drives the alarm.
His public line of **disbelief** hides real private fear.
His backup plan, **roofing**, is admittedly a panic, not a strategy.

steps.text: Put the flat purchase on hold and keep renting
Cancel the football season ticket and cut takeaways
Keep the deposit pot untouched as emergency money
Ask his uncle about learning roofing work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI and eight for robots. That I could live with a bit better. I'd be 35.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far enough off that we'll see. At work I'd probably joke about it. I'm not someone who goes on about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still be scared, but slower scared. Nadia would have time to move into something safer, maybe the management side of retail. I'd have time to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving. With eight years before the robots, I'd still buy the flat, just a smaller one with a shorter mortgage. I'd wait to see how the first care robots actually do before I learn anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a dull ache than a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, would you still hold off the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd buy, but smaller, so a lower mortgage we could pay off faster. That way if I lose work at 35, we're not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the roofing idea still come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, closer to the time. If I see robots in care in 2032 or so, I'd ring my uncle. Not before.

say: I'd say it's **far enough off** that we'll see.
I'd mostly **joke about it** at work rather than plan out loud.
think: I think I'd still be scared, just **slower scared**.
I think Nadia would have **time to move** into safer work.
do: Keep working and **saving** at the current pace.
Buy a **smaller flat** with a shorter mortgage.
Wait for the **first care robots** before learning anything new.
feel: **Anxious**, like a **dull ache** rather than a punch.
S3.quote: With eight years before the robots, I'd still buy the flat, just a smaller one with a shorter mortgage.
fieldNote: More time turns his plan from **cancel** to **downsize**.
He still expects to **lose work** around 35.
He'd **wait** for evidence before any retraining, true to type.

steps.text: Buy a smaller flat with a shorter mortgage
Keep saving each month alongside Nadia
Wait until care robots appear before calling his uncle about roofing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and then thirteen for robots. I'd be 40. That's half a career away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's so far off it might not happen. At work, nothing really. With mates, maybe a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years is long enough that I'd probably ignore it for ten, and I know that's daft. I'd probably carry on as normal and then panic in my late thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Nadia as planned. I'd keep doing my calls. Maybe in five or six years I'd look at a course in something like plumbing, if the robots start showing up in hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in the back of my head, calm on the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ignore it. What would make you not ignore it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it. If a mate in a care home said a robot was doing the lifting, I'd move. Not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from your agency in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of honesty from Mrs Holloway. If she's planning to buy robots, tell us early so we can plan too.

say: I'd say it's **so far off** it might not happen.
With mates I'd probably just **shrug** about it.
think: I think I'd **ignore it** for years, and I know that's daft.
I think I'd carry on and then **panic** in my late thirties.
do: Buy the **flat** with Nadia as planned.
Keep doing my **care calls** as normal.
Look at a **plumbing course** in five or six years.
S4.quote: Thirteen years is long enough that I'd probably ignore it for ten, and I know that's daft.
fieldNote: He's honest that **a decade of warning** would likely be wasted.
He'd only act on **seeing robots** in care himself.
He wants **early honesty** from his small agency's owner.

steps.text: Keep doing the same Holloway care calls
Buy the flat with Nadia on the original plan
Look into a plumbing course around year five or six

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd hit Nadia first and then me, and we'd lose the flat plan. What would help is warning from the agency and some help paying for a trade course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that care is a real skill. I've been doing this six years and I've never once wished I had a computer with me in a client's bathroom.

headlineQuote: I've been doing this six years and I've never once wished I had a computer with me in a client's bathroom.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old carer** at a small family agency, often booked for **older men's** personal care.
He lives with his girlfriend Nadia, a **phone shop manager**, and they're saving for a flat.
He's **pragmatic** and dislikes change, avoiding new tools unless made to use them.
He feels safe in AI Plateau but worries most about **Nadia's job**, which thinking AI hits first.
With fast robots he's **alarmed** and would shelve the flat; with more time, he'd likely **wait**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting Nadia first and then him, ending the flat plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** from the agency and help paying for a **trade course**.
